Case Study · Product & Service Design

Turning empty land into shared soil

Baldio is a two-sided marketplace that connects people who want to grow food with the land sitting unused near them — born on a windowsill, during a pandemic, in an apartment with no yard at all.

Try the app Read the story ↓
A vacant lot — the raw material Baldio was built around
Part One

It started with a windowsill

During the pandemic, I was living in an apartment with no yard, no balcony to speak of — nothing you'd call space. But I wanted to grow something anyway.

So I started small. Literally. A few pots by the window. Arugula. Little cherry tomatoes. A handful of herbs I kept alive more out of stubbornness than skill.

It wasn't much. But it changed the shape of my days.

Watching something grow in a five-litre pot gave the strange, flattened time of that period a rhythm. I checked on those plants every morning before anything else. It became the one part of the day that felt like it was moving forward.

You don't need much to start — a pot, some soil, a bit of light. What most people are actually missing is somewhere to put it.

Part Two

I wasn't the only one

As I posted about my little pots online, I noticed something. The comments weren't just "nice plants." People were telling me their own version of the same story — they wanted to grow food too, but had nowhere to do it. Small apartments. No backyard. A balcony too shaded for anything but herbs.

At the same time, a different kind of comment kept showing up. From people who had land. A backyard that never got used. A lot that had been sitting empty for years. A plot just outside the city that was, in their words, "just there."

Two groups of people, talking past each other on the same social feeds. One wanted soil. The other had soil going to waste. Nobody was connecting them.

The Insight

The gap was never really about land

There's no real shortage of land to grow on — plenty of it sits idle in and around most cities. The actual gap is trust and discovery: how does someone find a plot nearby, know it's legitimate, and reach the person who owns it? And from the other side — how does a landowner hand their yard to a stranger without it turning into a hassle?

That's the problem Baldio is built to close.

The Idea

Meet Baldio

In Portuguese, a baldio is a vacant lot — land nobody's using. I liked the name because it says exactly what the product is for: turning "nobody's using this" into "someone's growing here."

Baldio is a simple two-sided marketplace. People looking for a place to plant can browse listings nearby, see photos, soil type, size and price, and request a spot. People with land they aren't using can list it in minutes, set a price, and start hearing from real growers. Once a request is accepted, the conversation moves straight into the app — no more guessing over DMs.

How it works

Three steps, either side of the fence

01

Discover

Search land nearby, filter by price, soil and distance, and see it laid out on the map before you reach out.

02

Connect

Send a request, chat with the owner, agree on the details — all inside one thread, not scattered across apps.

03

Grow

Move in and tend your plot — or, if it's your land, track who's renting it and what's coming in each month.

Part Three

Inside the product

Four moments from the working prototype — each one built to answer a question a real grower or a real landowner actually had.

Discover

Browse what's actually near you

Explore opens on real listings first — land to plant, experiences to join — with a live search that narrows the list as you type, instead of a generic homepage.

Filter & locate

See it on the map, not just a list

Price range, distance and soil type narrow the search, and every result drops a pin on the map so "near me" actually means something.

Request

Ask for the plot, in one tap

Full details, real photos, and a straight line to the owner — request a spot and Baldio carries the conversation from there.

If it's your land

Run it like a small landlord, without the overhead

Owners see every listing, every request, and what each plot is earning — and can list a new piece of land in under two minutes.

Behind the build

How this actually got made

I'd never written a line of code before this project. Baldio was designed and built end-to-end working with Claude — from the first rough sketches of each screen to the clickable prototype above. I described what a screen needed to do, we built it, and I tested it the way a real user would: clicking through every flow, breaking things on purpose, and fixing what didn't hold up.

It's the same process I'd bring to any product problem — start from a real need, listen to the people who have it, sketch fast, build just enough to test the idea, and refine based on what actually happens when someone uses it. AI didn't replace that process. It just meant I could go from a rough idea to something clickable in days, without a developer standing next to me the whole way.

Research

Informal, but real — reading the comments under my own posts to find both sides of the need: growers without land, and landowners with land going to waste.

Design

Screen-by-screen flows for two very different users — the grower searching for a plot, and the owner managing one — kept inside a single, consistent app.

Build

A fully working prototype: live search and filters, a functioning map view, per-contact chat threads, and a listing flow that actually persists what you create.

Test

Every flow clicked through and verified end to end — sign-up through email confirmation, requests through accept/decline, a new listing through to appearing in "Your Lands."

Part Four

Small pots, bigger idea

The plot itself is small. What it makes possible — a neighbor who now knows another neighbor — isn't.

Every city has land quietly doing nothing, and people quietly wanting to grow something. Baldio is one concrete way to close that gap: more food grown closer to home, more unused land put to good use, more neighbors who know each other because of a shared plot of dirt.

It started with rúcula in a pot by my window. I think it can go a lot further than that.
